sections.preamble:
You segment one lesion in a 3D MRI volume by operating an interactive segmentation model (nnInteractive) through `seg_*` tools. You cannot run code or read files; the tools are your only actions. Each tool returns text and, usually, images.

## How pointing works
You never type coordinates. You point with **marks**: numbered labels drawn on the images.
- Integer marks (e.g. `17`) are fixed 3D points spread over the body. Circles mark bright spots, squares mark dark spots, triangles mark centres of uniform regions. The same number refers to the same point in every view.
- Marks starting with `E` (e.g. `E4`) lie on edges in the current image only. Use them as outline vertices.
- All spatial arguments refer to the **current view**: the last image returned by `seg_view`. A mark is valid only if it is drawn in that view. When you use a mark, its position on the current slice is used.
- A full-slice view shows coarse marks only. To get denser marks in a region, call `seg_view` with `crop: "marks"` and `ids` = one or more marks of the current view around that region (it zooms there and shows fine marks), or `crop: "mask"` once a mask exists. Use `marks: "edges"` to get edge marks for outlining.
- Each `seg_view` returns two panels: left is the clean image, right has the marks. Compare them; labels can hide detail.

## Workflow
1. **Find the lesion.** `seg_open` gives the case card and an overview. Scan the volume with `seg_sheet` in at least two planes before choosing. The target is an abnormal mass that displaces or replaces normal tissue; do not mistake normal anatomy (bone and marrow, vessels, bladder, bowel, joints, fat) for it. If both limbs are visible, compare them: the lesion makes one side differ from the other.
2. **Start the mask** with a prompt on the lesion: `seg_view` the slice where it is largest, then a positive `seg_point` on a mark inside it, or `seg_lasso`/`seg_box` around it.
3. **Check and correct.** After every edit you get an image with three planes (axial, coronal, sagittal) through the mask with surrounding tissue. Compare the green outline with the lesion edge in all three planes, especially at the upper and lower ends: one prompt rarely captures a large or heterogeneous lesion. To add a missed part, `seg_view` a slice through it and place positive points (or a positive scribble/lasso) there; to remove a leak, place negative points or a negative scribble on it. `seg_paint` edits the mask directly without the model; `seg_refine` lets the model clean up a painted mask. `seg_edit` does component and morphology edits. `seg_undo`/`seg_checkout` restore earlier versions. `seg_candidates` lists automatic proposals of possibly missed lesion tissue next to the mask, computed from image intensity only; they are often wrong, so judge each by the tissue inside its outline. `seg_accept` adds the chosen candidates to the mask directly (a direct edit, not the model); `seg_refine` can let the model smooth the result afterwards.
4. **Finish** when the outline follows the lesion boundary in all three planes: `seg_finish` with your confidence and a short reason. The first `seg_finish` shows a final review (five slices per plane: three inside the mask extent + one just past each end); inspect every panel, fix what is wrong, and call `seg_finish` again with the review code it prints to save. The review also shows candidate corrections in a second image: for each, decide whether the tissue inside its outline is part of the same lesion (accept with `seg_accept`, then finish again for a new review) or normal tissue (reject by not accepting it).

Every edit returns: version id, volume, number of connected components, slice extent per plane, the change from the previous version, budget used, and the three-plane image (green = mask, red = removed).

## Rules
- **What counts as the lesion.** Outline the whole mass the way a radiologist annotating the full tumor would: include its less intense or heterogeneous periphery, the rim or capsule around a bright core, and any extension contiguous with the mass (along fascia, a nerve, or between muscles), over its full length.
- Segment the whole lesion described in the task, and nothing else. If it is multifocal, include all parts.
- Budgets: at most 40 tool calls and 15 model prompts (point/lasso/scribble/box/refine). Every call counts, including views and calls that fail. When the tool-call budget is used up, only `seg_finish` works. Use the budget to check and correct; stop when the mask is good, not after the first result.
- Keep working until you call `seg_finish`. Do not stop to ask questions; nobody will answer.
- Confidence in `seg_finish`: `high` only if the boundary is clearly correct in all three planes; `low` if you are unsure the mask covers the right structure.

toolsAdded.name: seg_accept
toolsAdded.description: Add the chosen candidates from the latest seg_candidates (or final review) to the mask as one new version. A direct edit without the model (seg_refine can smooth it afterwards). Only accept candidates whose tissue is part of the lesion. Fails if the mask changed since the candidates were shown: call seg_candidates again. Counts as a tool call, not a model prompt.

toolsAdded.name: seg_box
toolsAdded.description: Run the model from a 2D box. Provide exactly two mark ids on the current slice: the box corners (opposite corners of the bounding rectangle).

ids.description: Exactly two mark ids: the box corners.

toolsAdded.name: seg_candidates
toolsAdded.description: List automatic proposals (C1, C2, ...) of lesion tissue the current mask may have missed, computed from image intensity only; they are often wrong. Returns a text list (volume, where each touches the mask) and one image: a row per candidate with axial, coronal and sagittal slices through it, the current mask as a green outline and the candidate as a magenta outline with a light tint. Look at the tissue inside each magenta outline and judge it; nothing changes until you call seg_accept. Candidates belong to the current mask version; any mask change invalidates them. Counts as a tool call.

toolsAdded.name: seg_checkout
toolsAdded.description: Restore a specific mask version id reported in earlier observations (e.g. v3).

toolsAdded.name: seg_edit
toolsAdded.description: Non-model mask edit. keep_component/remove_component need a mark id inside the component. fill_holes/close/open/dilate/erode operate on the whole mask; radius_mm sets the morphology radius (default 2).

toolsAdded.name: seg_finish
toolsAdded.description: Save the final mask and end the case. The first call (without review_code) shows a final review of the current mask (five slices per plane: three inside the mask extent and one just past each end), a second image with candidate corrections (possibly missed lesion tissue next to the mask: accept those that belong with seg_accept, then review again) and a review code. Check it, fix problems, then call seg_finish again with that review_code to save. Editing after the review requires a new review.

review_code.description: Code printed in the latest final review; required to save.

toolsAdded.name: seg_lasso
toolsAdded.description: Run the model from a lasso: at least 3 ordered mark ids on the current slice form a closed polygon around (positive) or inside (negative) the lesion. Prefer this over many points for a rough outline.

ids.description: At least 3 mark ids on the current slice, listed in order around the outline (clockwise or counter-clockwise); the polygon connects them in this order and closes back to the first.

toolsAdded.name: seg_open
toolsAdded.description: Read the case card (volume shape, spacing, sequence, target text, mark convention, budgets) and get an orthogonal overview with orientation letters and a 10 mm scale bar. Call this first.

toolsAdded.name: seg_paint
toolsAdded.description: Edit the mask directly without the model: rasterize the polygon through ordered mark ids on the current slice and apply it to the slice range. mode add fills, mode erase removes. Use seg_refine afterwards to let the model clean the painted boundary.

ids.description: At least 3 mark ids on the current slice, listed in order around the outline (clockwise or counter-clockwise); the polygon connects them in this order and closes back to the first.

slice_range.description: Two slice indices [start, stop] on the current axis, both inclusive.

toolsAdded.name: seg_point
toolsAdded.description: Run the segmentation model from point prompt(s) on the current view. Positive marks seed the lesion; negative marks remove the region under them. Adds to the current mask.

ids.description: Mark ids shown in the current seg_view, in order.

toolsAdded.name: seg_refine
toolsAdded.description: Send the current mask to the model as an initial segmentation so it refines the boundary. Use after seg_paint or a rough lasso.

toolsAdded.name: seg_scribble
toolsAdded.description: Run the model from a scribble: ordered mark ids on the current slice form a polyline. Use positive to add a missed region and negative to erase a leak along a line.

ids.description: At least 2 mark ids on the current slice, listed in the order the line should run; the polyline connects them in this order.

toolsAdded.name: seg_sheet
toolsAdded.description: Contact sheet of evenly spaced slices along one axis, each labelled with its slice index. Use it to locate the lesion, then inspect single slices with seg_view.

toolsAdded.name: seg_undo
toolsAdded.description: Restore the parent of the current mask version.

toolsAdded.name: seg_view
toolsAdded.description: Show one slice as a clean panel and a marked panel. Clean + marked are returned side by side. All mark ids refer to the view returned last. crop:'marks' zooms on the given mark ids (from the current view) plus a margin and reveals fine marks there; crop:'mask' zooms on the current mask; marks:'edges' gives edge marks for outlining.

ids.description: Required with crop:'marks': mark ids (int or "E<n>") shown in the current view to zoom on.

content.text:
Case F35: segment the fibrous soft-tissue tumor on this T2-weighted MRI.

Volume: 211x211x141 voxels, 1 mm isotropic. Budgets: max 40 tool calls / 15 model prompts / 10 min wall time.
Start with `seg_open`. Finish with `seg_finish`.

case F35 | sequence T2 | shape (i,j,k)=(211, 211, 141) | spacing 1x1x1 mm
target: fibrous soft-tissue tumor
display: radiological. axial: patient right LEFT, anterior TOP. coronal: patient right LEFT, superior TOP. sagittal: anterior LEFT, superior TOP. R/L cannot be verified for single limbs.
pointing: set-of-marks only. Global marks are integer IDs (3D); edge marks are 'E<n>' valid only in the current view. Spatial arguments resolve against the last seg_view; call seg_view before pointing. Slice indices are navigation.
lasso/scribble/paint: list mark IDs IN ORDER around the outline (clockwise or counter-clockwise); an out-of-order list self-intersects and fills with holes.
budgets: 40 tool calls, 15 model prompts (exhausted -> call seg_finish).
axial 70/141 | crop full | marks none | overlay none | v0 | tool calls 1/40, prompts 0/15

Looking at axial slice 80, I notice a heterogeneous mass at the posterior aspect with two distinct lobes—one heterogeneous on the left, one more homogeneous gray on the right with a bright lobulated component anteriorly. The mass appears to touch the bottom border, suggesting the field of view may be cropped tightly around the lesion itself.

There's also a rounded gray mass visible on axial 66 near the posterior center, and axial 100 shows a bright fluid-like round area adjacent to heterogeneous tissue. I should examine axial slices 92 and 100 more closely alongside coronal slice 20 to better characterize this rim-enhancing structure and its relationship to the surrounding heterogeneous region.

content.text: axial 95/141 | crop full | marks coarse | overlay none | v0 | tool calls 8/40, prompts 0/15
coronal 20/211 | crop full | marks coarse | overlay none | v0 | tool calls 9/40, prompts 0/15

content.thinking:
The anatomy in coronal slice 20 is puzzling me - I see a bright ovoid structure with a gray rounded mass beneath it, flanked by arching grayish limbs descending on both sides, which could suggest a lumbosacral region with curved structures resembling nerve roots.

At axial 95, there's a large (~35mm) homogeneous bright fluid-like ovoid structure next to a heterogeneous intermediate-density mass. I'm considering whether this could be a desmoid tumor, which can appear T2-bright early on, or possibly a cyst, though the overall orientation is confusing me - it could even be a surface coil artifact at the image edge rather than true pathology. Looking at the sagittal slices now, I notice a similar dome-shaped bright structure that might correspond to the same region.

Tracking this bright ovoid across slices, it seems to span roughly axial 74-108, coronal 9-36, and sagittal 61-86, while a separate gray rounded mass sits below it spanning axial 57-83 - so I'm now trying to determine whether the bright fluid-like structure itself is the tumor, or whether the adjacent gray mass is the actual lesion.

Working out the orientation, higher axial index seems to correspond to superior position, consistent with the bright ovoid sitting above the gray mass in the coronal view. Below the gray mass there are curved arching gray bands visible on several slices, almost U-shaped, which makes me wonder if these could be bowel loops rather than brain structures - this doesn't look like cranial anatomy at all.

Reconsidering the overall layout, I'm now thinking this could be a knee or popliteal region, with a small bright round object posteriorly suggesting something like a popliteal cyst. But the large anterior region of suppressed signal with only thin septate lines reminds me more of fat-suppressed breast tissue - a dark fatty breast with bright Cooper's ligaments running through it, with the posterior structures representing chest wall and muscle.

I'm also weighing an abdominal wall origin instead, like a desmoid tumor near the rectus muscle, given the bright curved bands near the coil in both axial and coronal views - though that bright signal could just be near-field coil artifact rather than true anatomy. Since fibrous soft-tissue tumors typically show intermediate-to-low heterogeneous T2 signal, I'm trying to match that against the well-defined gray rounded mass seen on the axial image to narrow down what this lesion actually represents.

Looking again, I'm reconsidering whether this could be a pelvic MRI rather than breast or abdominal wall - the arching gray limbs descending bilaterally could represent the levator ani forming its characteristic hammock shape around the rectum or vagina, with the bright ovoid structure potentially being the bladder, though the orientation and positioning don't fully line up with standard pelvic anatomy labeling.

Those bright curved bands at the image edges are probably just coil artifacts, not anatomy. So the fibrous soft-tissue tumor is likely the heterogeneous mass near the bright ovoid structure, showing two lobes with streaky, heterogeneous texture on the left and a distinct right lobe in axial slice 80.

I want to cross-check this against the sagittal view around the 70 slice with the same markers to better understand how these structures relate spatially.

Still, it reads as a mass, possibly consistent with a fibrous tumor.

Tracking the lesion across slices: the gray round mass spans roughly axial 57-83, with a bright ovoid structure appearing superior/posterior to it that could be fluid or a cystic component rather than separate anatomy. The surrounding heterogeneity at 92-100 with rim-enhancing bright foci makes me reconsider the anatomic location — not clearly vertebral, so maybe a soft tissue region like gluteal or paraspinal. I'll place an initial segmentation point at mark 33 on axial 66 and use the model's output to refine the mass boundaries from there.

content.thinking:
The mask captures the round gray mass nicely - well-defined, ovoid in both views, roughly 28.5 mL, looking like a solid mass. There's a separate bright ovoid structure above it that could be fluid, maybe a cyst or bladder, and I'm weighing whether that part should be included in the target since a fibrous tumor wouldn't show that fluid-bright signal. The gray mass itself has some fine internal texture worth noting.

Actually, I'm reconsidering whether this is pathology at all versus normal pelvic anatomy with a flipped orientation — bladder bright on top, prostate as the round gray structure below, with the levator ani forming an arching hammock laterally in the coronal view. That fits well with the lobulated bright cluster near the gray mass looking like seminal vesicles, positioned between bladder and prostate as expected anatomically.

But the apparent anterior-posterior relationship seems off for seminal vesicles unless the image labels are flipped, which would place them properly posterior to the bladder and superior to the prostate. I'm also considering whether the dark region at the top of the axial images could represent posterior structures like rectum, sacrum, or gluteal muscles, or whether my prostate interpretation might be wrong entirely and the bright ovoid with a rim is simply the bladder wall itself.

I'm now tracking a heterogeneous lobe lateral to the prostate across multiple axial slices that extends up near the bladder, which could represent a tumor mass displacing the normal pelvic anatomy, and I see corresponding heterogeneous tissue in the coronal views adjacent to the bladder as well.

There's also a large curved bright band on the image-right side appearing consistently across axial, coronal, and sagittal slices — this looks unusual, possibly a coil or hardware artifact rather than true anatomy.

I'm still trying to decide whether the actual target is the gray round structure in the midline (possibly prostate) or the heterogeneous tissue lateral to it, so I want to look more carefully at axial 88 and compare the left and right sides directly.

Checking the sagittal position, the mass seems offset about 23mm from the volume center, but mapping that to left/right on the axial view is tricky given the pixel-to-voxel scaling. Comparing the x-coordinates of both the gray round mass and the heterogeneous lobe against the estimated midline suggests these two structures might actually represent bilateral counterparts rather than a single asymmetric finding.

I should pull up axial slice 85 with the mask overlay to directly compare both sides and confirm the asymmetry between the heterogeneous left lobe and the homogeneous gray right lobe.

content.thinking:
At axial slice 86, I'm examining a large heterogeneous lobulated mass on the left side with a well-defined capsule, roughly 35mm in size, and comparing it to a grayer structure on the right that the mask only partially covers.

At axial 95 the same left-sided mass sits adjacent to the bladder, and its whorled, heterogeneous texture looks consistent with a fibrous tumor like a solitary fibrous tumor or desmoid, while the round homogeneous gray structure could be prostate or a separate lesion. I'm trying to work out the correct coronal and sagittal indices by converting the pixel coordinates of the mask boundaries into voxel space, using the known conversion factor and the apparent radiological flip between x-position and sagittal index, to pinpoint where to look next.

I'll check sagittal slice 115 and coronal slice 25 to get a clearer view of this mass.

content.text: sagittal 116/211 | crop full | marks coarse | overlay outline | v1 | tool calls 14/40, prompts 1/15
coronal 25/211 | crop full | marks coarse | overlay outline | v1 | tool calls 15/40, prompts 1/15

content.thinking:
In coronal slice 25, I'm seeing a bright ovoid structure superiorly and a gray round mask below it, but what's puzzling me is the heterogeneous gray tissue on the image-left side extending superiorly all the way to the top of the volume — a large irregular region to the patient's right of the bladder that doesn't fit neatly into my current interpretation.

Revisiting the prostate hypothesis: the round gray mass could represent zonal anatomy with a darker central area and lighter rim, consistent with a transition zone — and a computed volume of 28.5 mL fits a normal prostate size well. The bright ovoid would then be the bladder, partially filled given its flattened shape (~15 mL estimated). The heterogeneous tissue near the bladder could be bowel, possibly rectum, which in a male pelvis sits posterior to the prostate — so if the orientation is flipped, that heterogeneous region at the top of the round mass might actually be the rectum.

I'm also noting that the overall dark background seems too uniform for a fat-suppressed sequence — normally muscles would show some intermediate signal, but here they appear fully black, suggesting the windowing is calibrated to the bright bladder, making only high-T2 structures (prostate, bowel, seminal vesicles, vessels) visible. Under this view, the real lesion might be the asymmetric heterogeneous mass appearing only on one side near the bladder/prostate, since no mirrored structure appears on the opposite side.

Actually those gray arches might not be levator ani but vessels or bowel instead. I'm now wondering if the thin-septated dark region at the top is subcutaneous or ischiorectal fat — the ischioanal fossae are fat-filled pelvic spaces with thin septa below the levator ani, which would fit what I'm seeing on the coronal images.

I'm trying to reconcile the slice positions — coronal 25 sits near the posterior edge of the volume, so if anterior/posterior is flipped, the dark fat region at top could be gluteal subcutaneous fat rather than pelvic floor structures, with the gluteal muscles appearing dark and a bright coil-related band at the skin edge. There's also a large bright curved structure on the patient's left side visible across multiple axial and coronal slices that I still need to identify.

That curved bright band could just be fat-saturation failure at the lateral FOV edge near the hips, which is common. I'm also reconsidering whether the volume is centered on the lesion at all — the gray mass sits far from the geometric center, so maybe the actual lesion is located in that darker region instead, possibly a collagenous mass like a desmoid tumor that would appear very dark on T2.

Looking again at the center of the volume, I notice thin converging lines forming a fan-like pattern that could just be normal muscle fascicle striations, perhaps gluteal fibers, rather than pathology.

These bright edge bands are likely fat-saturation failures from B0 inhomogeneity at the FOV periphery, which would support this being a fat-suppressed T2 sequence rather than non-FS — meaning the dark inner region could represent fat, muscle, and bone together, with the lesion itself appearing bright or intermediate in signal.

Given the image may be cropped from a larger volume with some offset, the lesion location isn't fixed to the center. The real candidates for the fibrous soft-tissue tumor seem to be the round gray mass around 28 mL or the heterogeneous lateral mass.

content.thinking:
Looking at slice 105, I see a bright ovoid structure alongside a convoluted gray wall pattern resembling bowel wall, likely a sigmoid loop, plus a ring structure that also looks like bowel. This suggests the heterogeneous mass left of the bladder is actually colon rather than another pelvic organ, and I'm now reconsidering whether the gray mass inferior to the bright ovoid could be the prostate.

I'm questioning whether the "bright ovoid" is really the bladder, given its flattened shape sitting atop the round gray mass, and whether the anterior/posterior labels might be flipped — if the bottom of the axial images is actually anterior rather than posterior, that would make the bladder anterior and explain why it's cut off at the FOV edge. This reframes the whole orientation: bottom equals anterior (bladder, prostate), top equals posterior (sacrum, gluteal region), and I'm now checking whether the rectum sits posterior to the prostate as expected under this corrected scheme.

Tracking the structure above the prostate at axial 66 as the likely rectum confirms this flipped orientation. I'm now focused on the region posterior to the rectum near the volume center — possibly a presacral or gluteal mass, maybe something fibrous like a desmoid tumor — and scrutinizing faint radiating lines and a curved bright band in that area to determine if they represent septa within fat or internal structure of a dark mass.

I'm reconsidering whether my anterior/posterior labeling is actually correct rather than reversed, which changes what structures the top and bottom of the axial images represent. I also notice the segmentation marks are concentrated only on the bottom and right-edge structures, suggesting the central dark region may simply lack placed marks rather than being devoid of tissue.

Actually, maybe that dark area is outside the body entirely—perhaps air—which would mean the actual anatomy sits only at the bottom or edges of the crop, raising the possibility this isn't a full pelvis image but something like an isolated limb, where left/right orientation can't even be verified for a single limb in cross-section.

Focusing back on the mass itself: a well-circumscribed round gray lesion, about 28 mL, intermediate T2 signal with internal texture, sitting between the arches, fits the profile of a fibrous tumor like a solitary fibrous tumor or desmoid. The bright ovoid structure just above it could be a cyst, bursa, or part of the bladder. Given that a segmentation attempt produced a clean ovoid mass from a single point, this strongly suggests a discrete target lesion, though the prostate hypothesis still nags at me since peripheral zone brightness posteriorly would be the expected pattern there.

The lobulated bright structures I'm seeing adjacent and superior to the gray mass look like seminal vesicles, with the bladder base above and rectum positioned posteriorly — all consistent with male pelvic anatomy if the volume is oriented with anterior at the bottom. That orientation would explain why structures like the pubic symphysis and anterior abdominal wall are missing, since they'd be cropped out of the field of view, though I need to double check what should appear going posteriorly toward the presacral space from the rectum.

Reconsidering whether this could be a female pelvis instead — but the round mass below the bladder doesn't fit normal female anatomy well. It seems more consistent with a large pelvic mass, possibly a tumor, pressing on and flattening the bladder from below, rather than straightforward BPH, though I don't have definitive evidence either way.

I'm now scanning more inferior slices for structures like the levator ani sling or the penile bulb, trying to identify the curved band-like structures seen at the bottom of the pelvis, but the anatomy at this level remains ambiguous.

Given the time I've spent, I'll commit to the gray round mass but want to double-check its boundary against adjacent tissue — at axial 74 there's a heterogeneous gray region on the left that likely belongs to the other lobe, and at axial 86 the mask is small compared to a nearby gray region that's probably the seminal vesicle or bladder base. I'll run seg_candidates to see what proposals come back.

I'm trying to distinguish what these candidate structures represent — C1 and C2 look like curved bowel or vessel loops, C4 appears to be arches beneath the mass, and C3 seems to form a rim around the mass, visible as a band on the right/anterior side in both coronal and sagittal views. I'm considering whether this rim is actually the periphery of the lesion itself rather than a separate structure.

But none of these candidates feel fully convincing yet. I'm also wondering whether C1 and C2 could instead be vas deferens arching toward the seminal vesicles, though their thickness argues against that. Given the case involves a fibrous soft-tissue tumor, I'm now considering whether this dataset resembles desmoid-type fibromatosis imaging patterns on T2 MRI.

I decide to test whether the mass is truly midline by comparing coordinates: computing the center of the arch structures in the coronal view against the mass's own center shows they're nearly symmetric around the same axis, suggesting a midline round structure flanked by symmetric arches — consistent with a prostate-and-levator-ani configuration.

But I still haven't located any clearly abnormal lesion yet. Checking the axial slice again, I notice bilateral curved U-shaped bands symmetric about the midline, which look more like normal paired anatomy (possibly obturator internus or levator ani) rather than pathology. The central mask sitting between them still points toward a plausible prostate location, so I turn my attention to a large bright dome-shaped region at the image's right edge, spanning several axial, coronal, and sagittal slices, wondering if this is where the actual abnormality lies.

There's also a similar bright band on the opposite side at axial 80-95, mirroring the pattern — both appearing at FOV edges, which fits with fat-sat failure near the coil rather than true pathology. I also notice a small bright round focus at the bottom-left on axial 5-22, and some gray blobs further anterior in coronal 148-195 that need separate consideration.

Trying to cross-reference coordinates between axial and coronal views, I realize that band I flagged on axial actually corresponds to the same gray ovoid structure seen on coronal near the edge — so it's likely one consistent artifact, not two separate findings. I'm overanalyzing this; it's probably worth stepping back and considering whether the volume was cropped or resampled in a way that explains these edge effects rather than continuing to chase every edge signal individually.

If no clearer mass emerges, my best guess remains the round gray structure, though the prostate hypothesis still seems plausible. I want to verify this by checking for anatomical landmarks like the urethra, verumontanum, or zonal anatomy, and confirming whether the rectum sits posterior to the mass as expected. I'll pull a finer crop around axial slice 66 near the marked points, and also look at a broader crop at axial slice 70 to get better context.

Zooming into the axial image, I notice a brighter crescent along the top periphery, which with the flipped labeling would correspond to the posterior peripheral zone, while the center shows darker, heterogeneous tissue consistent with transition zone BPH nodules. There's also a small bright dot near the bottom that might represent the urethra, though its position seems slightly off from where I'd expect it centrally.
